origem: Items: [inference] in question form; the practice assessed comes from the book (PDF pages indicated). The book has NO checklist or maturity model.

items.text: Is there a team (or person) dedicated to DPE, with its own goals and metrics?
Is there explicit executive sponsorship for the practice?
Do CI/CD decisions consider the effect on developer productivity, and not only auditability or vulnerability checks?
Is there a declared culture of continuously improving toolchain productivity?
Is the prioritization of improvements driven by data and not just by who complains the loudest?
Is the impact of the toolchain team's work visible (before/after, trend) to the organization?
Are local build time (with tests) and the frequency of builds per developer measured?
Does the local build with tests usually stay under ~10 minutes?
Is the local quality gate (tests before the push) preserved, without shifting feedback to after the pull request?
Are small, frequent changes encouraged by the workflow and the build speed?
Is CI feedback time (PR and integration branch) measured and tracked?
Is the local build cache enabled?
Is there a remote cache, written by CI and read by CI and local machines?
Has modularization been assessed (leaf modules, unstable modules with many dependents)?
Are volatile inputs (timestamps, non-reproducible generators) detected and eliminated?
Is the cache hit rate monitored per action/task?
Is the cache infrastructure (download bandwidth, storage) monitored?
Are toolchains (e.g., JVM version and vendor) standardized to avoid misses?
Is the fraction of build time spent on tests known?
Have implicit dependencies between tests and shared resources been addressed or isolated?
Is the available test parallelism (even on a single machine) enabled?
Has test distribution (or an alternative better than CI fanout) been evaluated?
Have very large test classes been identified and split when they limit balancing?
Does every toolchain run, local and CI, generate data that is collected centrally?
Are the median and percentiles (not just the mean) of build time tracked over windows of weeks?
Is it possible to compare two builds (failed vs. successful; hit vs. miss)?
Are I/O, memory and network bottlenecks (dependency downloads, disk, antivirus, latency to caches) measured?
Is there a durable, browsable record of each build with deep links?
Are failures classified into verification vs. non-verification?
Is the non-verification failure rate measured (open source project reference: 2-5% of builds, 3-10% of test builds)?
Is the owner of each failure type clear (developer vs. build/CI team)?
Is the failure list prioritized in this order: new frequent non-verification, old actionable, frequent verification, other quick ones?
Is the MTTR of build failures measured?
Are avoidable lint and formatting failures prevented (IDE auto-format, git hook)?
Are builds reproducible (declared inputs, no dependence on environment state)?
Are reliability regressions detected quickly, with visibility into who was affected?
Do developers rarely need to repeat the build, clear caches or re-clone the workspace to get unblocked?
Are flaky tests identified using run history (not just by reports)?
Is there a strategy of re-running in a different order, in isolation and in another environment to classify the cause?
Is there an explicit target of fewer than 1% of developer pipeline runs failing due to non-verification?
Is the probability of a flaky-free run (P_pass) estimated for the test suite?
Are retries used without masking flakiness (the test remains marked as flaky)?
Is there a quarantine for flaky tests that does not block integration?
Are there regular Flaky Fix-It Days?
Do new and modified tests go through aggressive retries to catch flakiness early?
Is the waiting cost of local and CI builds quantified with the organization's own data?
Is the debugging cost of code failures and build logic failures estimated?
Is the CI infrastructure cost known and linked to cache usage?
Have the book's example assumptions (US$ 1/min, 80% waiting) been replaced with the organization's data?
Have vendors' claimed gains (50-90% savings, hard ROI) been treated as hypotheses to validate?
